title: The origins of World War I
subtitle: Nationalism, imperial decline, alliances, and military planning
intro: The assassination at Sarajevo was the spark, but the reading explains why an apparently stable international order was vulnerable to a much larger war. German power, Ottoman decline, nationalism, alliances, and rigid mobilization plans connected the crisis in the Balkans to the great powers.

blocks.title: The chapter’s central problem
blocks.text: On June 28, 1914, Gavrilo Princip assassinated Archduke Franz Ferdinand and his wife in Sarajevo. The chapter introduction frames the resulting war as a rupture in the imperial order: a European conflict became global through the Ottoman Empire, Japan, colonial participation, and U.S. entry in 1917. The table of contents previews later topics; it is not itself a full reading on those topics.

blocks.title: Stability was deceptive
blocks.text: The early twentieth century brought economic growth and excitement about aircraft, automobiles, radio, and cinema. Yet Germany’s growing industry and armed forces challenged Britain at sea and France in Morocco. The Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905 ended in Japanese victory, showing that power was shifting beyond Europe too.

blocks.title: Ottoman decline and the Balkans
blocks.text: The Ottoman Empire fell behind stronger European states economically, technologically, and militarily. Territorial losses and nationalist movements created a power vacuum. Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1908; Italy took Libya in the war of 1911–1912; the Balkan Wars of 1912–1913 sharply reduced Ottoman territory in Europe. Rival states and nationalist movements competed over what would replace Ottoman authority.

blocks.title: The Young Turks
blocks.text: Reform-minded officers and other Young Turks challenged Sultan Abdul Hamid II and sought constitutional government. He was deposed in 1909. Reform and military modernization coexisted with centralization and Turkification, which alienated other ethnic communities. The reading emphasizes that modernizing an empire did not automatically resolve its internal national conflicts.

blocks.title: Nationalism both united and divided
blocks.text: National identification encouraged loyalty, military service, sacrifice, and confidence in a just cause. It could unite populations behind governments in France, Britain, Germany, and Italy. In the Russian, Austro-Hungarian, and Ottoman empires, however, national and religious minorities could challenge imperial rule. An independent Serbia encouraged the hopes of Slavic populations under Habsburg control.

blocks.title: Two rival alliance blocs
blocks.text: Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy formed the Triple Alliance in 1882. France allied with Russia, and Britain reached an entente with France in 1904 and with Russia in 1907. German dreadnought construction challenged British naval supremacy. These alignments meant that a Balkan dispute could involve much larger powers. Remember that Italy’s prewar alliance did not determine its eventual wartime side.

blocks.title: Military schedules narrowed choices
blocks.text: Huge armies depended on railways and precise timetables. France and Germany expected to mobilize quickly; Russia’s size and weaker rail network suggested a slower response. German planners hoped to defeat France through a sweep across Belgium, then move east before Russia was fully ready. Once mobilization began, leaders feared that delays would surrender an advantage. The reading treats these pressures as crucial, but military plans did not literally remove every political choice.

blocks.title: From Sarajevo to a European war
blocks.text: Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia on July 28, 1914. Russian support for Serbia and German support for Austria-Hungary widened the crisis. Germany declared war on Russia on August 1 and France on August 3. The invasion of neutral Belgium and Britain’s entry followed on August 4. The main connection is assassination → regional confrontation → mobilization and alliance commitments → a much wider war.

keyTerms.Nationalism: Identification with a national community; it can unite a state or undermine a multiethnic empire.
keyTerms.Entente: An understanding or diplomatic alignment; the term does not mean a single merged state.
keyTerms.Mobilization: Preparing and moving forces and resources for war.
keyTerms.Dreadnought: A heavily armed modern battleship associated with the naval arms race.
keyTerms.Young Turks: A reform movement that challenged Ottoman autocracy and pursued modernization and centralization.

connections: Compare the reading’s railway timetables with the slides’ Schlieffen Plan.
Explain why Serbia threatened Austria-Hungary even though Serbia was much smaller.
Distinguish the immediate trigger from the long-term causes.
notes: Some photographed edges and the chronology table are cropped. The notes cover the visible material.
The textbook compresses several dates: German troops crossed into Belgium on August 4, 1914 (not August 3). Russian partial mobilization on July 29 preceded the general mobilization order of July 30.
For the wider Balkan sequence, Albania declared independence in 1912; the page’s reference to an Ottoman loss of Albania in 1910 is misleading.

title: Industrial warfare and the home front
subtitle: Stalemate, civilian mobilization, and new tools of war
intro: Industrial weapons made prepared defenses extremely difficult to break. Armies became dependent on whole societies for supplies, labor, and money. The same war that trapped soldiers in trenches also transformed civilian work, imperial economies, communications, and technology.

blocks.title: Why the quick-war plans failed
blocks.text: Early offensives relied on confidence in movement and determined infantry attacks. German troops advanced through Belgium and northern France but became exhausted. French commander Joseph Joffre used a gap between German armies at the Marne in September 1914. The advance was checked, and both sides spread their defenses toward the North Sea.

blocks.title: How stalemate developed
blocks.text: The Western Front extended from the North Sea to the Swiss border. Machine guns were devastating against exposed infantry but difficult to move and set up during an assault. Soldiers built increasingly deep and connected trenches, with sandbags, planks, and communication routes. Attackers crossing no man’s land faced wire and fire; artillery preparation could warn defenders and give them time to reinforce.

blocks.title: Attrition in 1916
blocks.text: Verdun and the Somme illustrate the enormous cost of attempts to break the deadlock. The reading gives approximately 281,000 German losses and 315,000 French casualties at Verdun. For the Somme it lists 420,000 British casualties, including about 60,000 on the first day, alongside roughly 450,000 German and 200,000 French losses. These are the textbook’s estimates. Casualties are not the same as deaths.

blocks.title: Sea power and submarine warfare
blocks.text: Britain cut German overseas telegraph connections and blockaded the Central Powers. The German surface fleet rarely challenged the British fleet; Jutland in 1916 was the main confrontation and did not break the strategic deadlock. U-boats threatened shipping to Britain, while the sinking of the Lusitania in 1915 generated U.S. protests. Naval fighting therefore affected food, trade, neutral states, and civilian lives.

blocks.title: The war economy reached civilians
blocks.text: Armies required weapons, ammunition, and food on an unprecedented scale. Governments increased taxes, rationed goods, and directed production. Women filled jobs in transport, public services, factories, administration, and medical or military support. African, Indian, and Chinese laborers also worked in Europe. Some women gained income and a stronger sense of independence, although wartime opportunities did not automatically create lasting equality.

blocks.title: Hardship was unequal
blocks.text: The British blockade and poor harvests helped create severe German shortages. After the potato-crop failure of 1916, the “turnip winter” forced many people onto a meager diet; the text cites roughly 1,000 calories per day. Women, children, and older people were especially vulnerable. By contrast, need-based rationing in Britain and France could improve access to food for some poorer households.

blocks.title: Colonies and the United States
blocks.text: African territories faced military campaigns, requisitioning, taxation, forced labor, and demands for export crops. Africans served as soldiers and porters, while France recruited colonial troops. The United States profited from supplying Britain and France even before formally entering the war in 1917. War production, bonds, victory gardens, and new jobs tied American civilians to the conflict; employment helped drive African American migration from the rural South to northern cities.

blocks.title: New weapons had limits
blocks.text: Heavy artillery prepared attacks, but machine guns, grenades, and wire still favored defenders. Tanks first used in 1916 brought guns and armor across rough ground but often broke down. Aircraft and balloons observed enemy movements; aircraft and Zeppelins also carried bombs. Chemical weapons caused terrible suffering, while flamethrowers were constrained by short range and limited fuel. No single invention consistently solved the battlefield problem.

blocks.title: Communications, supplies, and camouflage
blocks.text: Field telephones improved coordination, though laying wire under fire was dangerous. Radio developed quickly, especially at sea, but fragile equipment and visible aerials limited field use. Concertina and other barbed wire strengthened defenses. Preserved field rations show the logistical effort behind mass armies. Artists helped disguise observation posts and equipment; Norman Wilkinson’s dazzle patterns made a ship’s course and speed harder for submarine crews to judge rather than simply making the ship invisible.

keyTerms.Stalemate: A military deadlock in which neither side can achieve a decisive breakthrough.
keyTerms.Attrition: Wearing down an opponent’s personnel, resources, and capacity to continue.
keyTerms.Blockade: An effort to prevent ships and supplies from reaching an enemy.
keyTerms.Home front: Civilian society and economic activity supporting and affected by the war.
keyTerms.Dazzle camouflage: Bold patterns intended to confuse estimates of a ship’s movement.
keyTerms.Victory garden: A civilian garden used to supplement wartime food supplies.

connections: Explain why more powerful weapons could prolong a war instead of shortening it.
Use women’s work, colonial labor, and rationing as evidence of total war.
Compare German food shortages with the United States’ economic gains.
notes: Numerical casualty estimates differ across sources. Any practice question using these figures identifies this reading and keeps casualties distinct from deaths.
The technology box has dating errors: the American Civil War began in 1861, and Britain used poison gas in 1915, not first in 1918.

The Lusitania page gives 139 American deaths; the widely accepted figure is 128. This guide does not test the incorrect figure. The visible start of the Ottoman-war section is incomplete, so the summary does not invent its missing continuation.

title: War’s end and an unsettled peace
subtitle: Peace treaties, the human cost, Russia, and the fragile 1920s
intro: This bundle moves between the end of fighting and the postwar settlement. Its central theme is that an armistice did not end instability: losses, displacement, rival national claims, revolution, economic crisis, and weak international cooperation all shaped the peace.

blocks.title: U.S. entry and the German gamble
blocks.text: Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare on February 1, 1917, hoping to defeat Britain before the United States could intervene effectively. Convoys protected by destroyers helped Britain keep supplies moving. The United States declared war on Germany on April 6. Germany’s gamble failed to win a decisive advantage before American manpower arrived.

blocks.title: The last campaigns and the armistice
blocks.text: Wilson presented the Fourteen Points in January 1918, calling for evacuation of occupied lands, settlement of territorial disputes, and an association of nations. Ludendorff’s spring offensives brought German forces near Paris but did not win the war. Increasing American arrivals and Allied counterattacks in August drove Germany back. Military setbacks, Ludendorff’s resignation, and naval mutinies accompanied political collapse. The ceasefire took effect at 11 a.m. on November 11, 1918.

blocks.title: Death, injury, and displacement
blocks.text: The text estimates that 9–10 million soldiers died and many more returned wounded, gassed, or psychologically traumatized. War, revolution, and border changes uprooted Russians, Germans, Hungarians, Greeks, Muslims, and other populations. France accepted migrants to rebuild its population, while U.S. restrictions in 1921 and 1924 limited immigration from parts of Europe. Battlefields, forests, farms, and towns required years of recovery.

blocks.title: The influenza pandemic
blocks.text: The 1918–1919 pandemic spread across a world linked by troop movements and transportation. Wartime censorship suppressed news in belligerent states, while reporting in neutral Spain helped produce the misleading name “Spanish flu.” The sidebar estimates about 50 million deaths worldwide and approximately 675,000 in the United States. The main text on the same page gives older, lower estimates, so these figures should not be combined as though they were a consistent count.

blocks.title: Who controlled the peace?
blocks.text: The Paris negotiations were dominated by Wilson, Lloyd George, and Clemenceau, even though the broader leadership group also included Italy’s Orlando. Defeated powers had little influence over the drafting, Russia was excluded, and smaller or colonized peoples struggled to be heard. Japan’s racial-equality proposal and Pan-African appeals illustrate the limits of universal-sounding principles when they challenged imperial power.

blocks.title: Versailles and national borders
blocks.text: Germany signed Versailles on June 28, 1919. The treaty imposed military restrictions, territorial losses, reparations, and a responsibility clause. France recovered Alsace-Lorraine; Poland was reconstituted; Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia emerged from the collapse of empires. The new states still contained dissatisfied minorities. The reading argues that the treaty produced humiliation without secure reconciliation; recognize that judgment as the author’s interpretation rather than a fact proved by the text alone.

blocks.title: The League’s promise and limits
blocks.text: Wilson wanted an organization to preserve peace and encourage cooperation. The U.S. Senate refused ratification of Versailles, and the United States never joined the League. The League could still work on health, labor, and communications, but its ability to enforce decisions against aggressive states was much weaker. Its practical achievements and its security failures should be distinguished.

blocks.title: Civil war and the Soviet Union
blocks.text: The Bolsheviks faced anti-communist forces supported by former Allied powers. Fighting, confiscation of crops, ruined infrastructure, and famine devastated Russia. By 1921 the Communists had defeated most major enemies, although the broader civil-war period extended beyond the text’s simplified starting point. The Soviet Union formed in 1922, incorporating Russia, Ukraine, Belarus, and the Transcaucasian federation. Finland, the Baltic states, and Poland remained outside it at this point.

blocks.title: The New Economic Policy
blocks.text: Lenin’s NEP allowed limited private trade and small-scale enterprise while the state retained major industries, banks, and railways. It was a tactical retreat from comprehensive state control to restore production after economic collapse. It did not mean abandoning Communist political rule or the long-term goal of industrialization. The policy began in 1921; the photographed page’s 1923 date is incorrect.

blocks.title: Stalin and Trotsky
blocks.text: After Lenin’s death in January 1924, Trotsky and Stalin competed for leadership. Trotsky stressed international revolution; Stalin emphasized “socialism in one country.” Stalin built support within the party bureaucracy, marginalized opponents, and forced Trotsky into exile in 1929. The reading connects this consolidation of power to the coming drive for rapid industrialization.

blocks.title: Hyperinflation and a fragile recovery
blocks.text: German reparations difficulties and French occupation of the Ruhr intensified the crisis of 1923. Printing money helped drive hyperinflation, eroding savings and social stability. Currency stabilization and international lending supported recovery after 1924. U.S. banks lent to Germany, Germany paid reparations to Britain and France, and those countries serviced U.S. wartime debts. This circular flow depended heavily on continued credit.

blocks.title: An “ephemeral” peace
blocks.text: Many Germans and Italians felt cheated, while Arabs, Indians, Chinese, and other peoples had unfulfilled expectations. German-Soviet cooperation showed that states excluded from the postwar order could work around it. Recovery and diplomacy produced a period of calm, but unresolved borders and dependence on credit made it fragile. The opening of the China–Japan section contrasts China’s instability with Japan’s state-led industrial and military development; the bundle provides only the beginning of that topic.

keyTerms.Armistice: An agreement to stop fighting; it is not the same as a final peace treaty.
keyTerms.Reparations: Payments or compensation required for war damage.
keyTerms.Self-determination: A people’s claim to determine its political status and government.
keyTerms.NEP: New Economic Policy: limited market activity under continuing Communist rule.
keyTerms.Hyperinflation: An extremely rapid rise in prices and collapse in a currency’s purchasing power.
keyTerms.Ephemeral: Short-lived; the reading uses it to characterize the unstable postwar peace.
keyTerms.USSR: Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, created in 1922.
